key_terms.meaning: Thyristor switch (two antiparallel SCRs or a TRIAC) in series with an AC load; it changes the RMS voltage, never the frequency.
V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π]; power factor = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>.
Angle at which the load current returns to zero; β = π for a resistor, β > π for an RL load; conduction angle γ = β − α.
φ ≤ α ≤ π with φ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R); below φ a short gate pulse is lost and the current gets a DC part.
n cycles on, m off: D = n/(n + m), V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D, PF = √D; subharmonics at 50/(n + m) Hz.
Q1 (MT2 +, gate +), Q2 (+, −), Q3 (−, −), Q4 (−, +); Q4 needs the most gate current.
Positive only: Q1 and Q4 (avoid). Negative only: Q2 and Q3. Following MT2 (DIAC): Q1 and Q3.
α ≈ tan⁻¹(ωRC) + sin⁻¹(V<sub>BO</sub>/V<sub>Cm</sub>), with V<sub>BO</sub> ≈ 30 V.
Six SCRs, no neutral: three and two conduct (0° to 60°), two (60° to 90°), two then none (90° to 150°); zero output at 150°.
A second gate pulse 60° after the first, so two SCRs in different lines are on together.
3rd, 9th, … orders, in phase in all three lines: they add in a neutral, circulate in a delta and cannot flow in balanced three-wire lines.
Series and freewheeling bidirectional switches at f<sub>sw</sub>: V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D, 50 Hz part V<sub>1</sub> = D V<sub>s</sub>, sidebands at m f<sub>sw</sub> ± f.
LC low-pass with corner between 50 Hz and f<sub>sw</sub>; raises the supply power factor from √D to close to 1.
P and N converter groups back to back; builds a new output frequency from pieces of the supply with no DC link.
α = cos⁻¹(r sin ω<sub>o</sub>t), so the local average (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α follows a sine; largest fundamental peak 2V<sub>m</sub>/π.
Step-down (f<sub>o</sub> < f<sub>s</sub>, usually ≤ f<sub>s</sub>/3) uses natural commutation; step-up (f<sub>o</sub> > f<sub>s</sub>) needs forced commutation.
Both groups fired with α<sub>P</sub> + α<sub>N</sub> = 180° and an intergroup reactor, or one group at a time with a dead time at current zero.
Nine bidirectional switches S<sub>Xy</sub> (18 IGBTs); exactly one closed per output, giving 27 states.
d<sub>Aa</sub> + d<sub>Ab</sub> + d<sub>Ac</sub> = 1 and v<sub>A</sub> = d<sub>Aa</sub>v<sub>a</sub> + d<sub>Ab</sub>v<sub>b</sub> + d<sub>Ac</sub>v<sub>c</sub> over T<sub>s</sub>.
q = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>in</sub> ≤ √3/2 = 0.866, because output line voltages must fit inside the narrowest input gap, 1.5 V<sub>im</sub>.

takeaways: An AC voltage controller changes only the RMS value; the output stays at the supply frequency.
With a resistor, V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π] and the power factor equals V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>, falling because of harmonics and a lagging fundamental.
With an RL load the SCRs conduct to β beyond π, control starts only at α = φ, and short gate pulses below φ give a one-way current.
On-off control gives V<sub>s</sub>√D with clean current while on, but subharmonics at 50/(n + m) Hz; it suits heaters, not lamps.
A TRIAC fires in all four quadrants, Q4 worst: use negative pulses (Q2 and Q3) or pulses that follow MT2 (Q1 and Q3), as a DIAC does.
A three-wire star controller has no neutral, so the phases interact, double pulses are needed and the output reaches zero at 150°, not 180°.
A PWM AC chopper moves the unwanted frequencies up to f<sub>sw</sub> ± 50 Hz; with an input filter its supply power factor is close to 1.
A cycloconverter builds a lower frequency from pieces of the supply with natural commutation; it needs two groups and suits large, slow drives.
A matrix converter changes voltage and frequency directly with nine bidirectional switches, regenerates naturally, and is limited to q ≤ 0.866.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask for a circuit, the waveforms at a stated firing angle and a derivation or calculation of the RMS output. The exam course stresses TRIAC triggering with positive and negative gate pulses, TRIAC-based phase controllers and the SCR configurations of single-phase and three-phase controllers; a few syllabi add cycloconverters, matrix converters and PWM AC choppers.

bank.q: Explain the working of a single-phase full-wave AC voltage controller feeding a resistive load. Define the firing angle and the conduction angle, sketch the supply voltage, gate pulses and load voltage for α = 60°, and derive the RMS output voltage.
outline: Circuit: two SCRs in antiparallel (or a TRIAC) in series with R across v<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin ωt
T1 conducts from α to π, T2 from π + α to 2π
Firing angle α and conduction angle π − α
Waveforms of v<sub>s</sub>, gate pulses, v<sub>o</sub> and the voltage across the SCRs
Derivation of V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π]
Limits α = 0 and α = π, and the power factor V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>
answer: Circuit. Two SCRs, T1 and T2, are connected in antiparallel and the pair is in series with the load resistor R across the supply v<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin ωt, where V<sub>m</sub> = √2 V<sub>s</sub>. A TRIAC can replace the pair. Each SCR turns off when its current falls to zero, so the supply commutates it.

Definitions. The firing angle α is the angle, measured from the zero crossing of the supply voltage, at which an SCR receives its gate pulse: T1 at α in the positive half cycle and T2 at π + α in the negative half. The conduction angle is the angle for which an SCR conducts; with a resistor the current is in phase with the voltage and ends at the voltage zero, so it is π − α.

answer.text: Operation over one cycle for α = 60°:

answer: Waveforms to sketch, one under another on the same θ axis from 0 to 2π: (a) the supply sine of peak V<sub>m</sub>; (b) short gate pulses of T1 at 60° and 420°, and of T2 at 240°; (c) the load voltage, zero from 0° to 60°, following the sine from 60° to 180°, zero from 180° to 240°, following the negative sine from 240° to 360°; the current has the same shape divided by R; (d) the voltage across the SCR pair, equal to v<sub>s</sub> while both are off and zero while one conducts. Shade the parts of the sine that reach the load.

answer.text: Derivation. Both half cycles are alike, so the mean square over one half cycle is enough:
answer.pre:
V<sub>o</sub>² = (1/π) ∫ from α to π of V<sub>m</sub>² sin²θ dθ
     = (V<sub>m</sub>²/2π) ∫ from α to π of (1 − cos 2θ) dθ
     = (V<sub>m</sub>²/2π) [θ − ½ sin 2θ] from α to π
     = (V<sub>m</sub>²/2π) [π − α + ½ sin 2α]
V<sub>o</sub> = (V<sub>m</sub>/√2) √[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π] = V<sub>s</sub> √[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π]

answer: Checks of the limits. At α = 0 the bracket is π/π = 1 and V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>, the full supply. At α = π the bracket is 0 and V<sub>o</sub> = 0. In between V<sub>o</sub> falls smoothly, so the whole range 0 ≤ α ≤ π is usable with a resistor. α must be in radians.

Power factor. P = V<sub>o</sub>²/R and the supply current equals the load current V<sub>o</sub>/R, so PF = (V<sub>o</sub>²/R)/(V<sub>s</sub>V<sub>o</sub>/R) = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = 0.897 at α = 60°. It is less than 1 even with a resistor, because the chopped current has harmonics and its 50 Hz part lags the voltage.

Closing check: the output is 206.3 V, which lies between 0 and 230 V, and squaring gives 206.3²/230² = 0.8045, the bracket value. The frequency of the output is still 50 Hz; only the RMS value changed.

bank.q: Describe on-off (integral-cycle) control of an AC load. Define the duty ratio D, derive the RMS output and the input power factor for a resistive load, and compare it with phase control. A 230 V, 20 Ω heater is switched on for 25 cycles out of every 100: find V<sub>o</sub>, the power, the power factor and the lowest frequency in the supply current.
outline: SCRs fired at the voltage zero for n cycles, blocked for m cycles
D = n/(n + m), V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D, PF = √D
Clean sine while on, low interference; subharmonics and flicker
Heaters, not lamps
answer: Principle. The antiparallel SCR pair (or TRIAC) is fired at the zero crossing of the supply voltage for n whole cycles, then left unfired for m whole cycles, and the pattern repeats. The load sees complete sine cycles or nothing. Because switching happens at the voltage zero, where a resistive load also has zero current, there is almost no switching interference.
Duty ratio. D = n/(n + m), the fraction of cycles in which the load is connected. The pattern period is (n + m) supply periods.

answer.text: RMS output. During the on cycles the load voltage is the full supply sine; during the off cycles it is zero. The mean square over one pattern period is therefore D times the mean square of the supply:
answer.pre:
V<sub>o</sub>² = [n/(n + m)] V<sub>s</sub>² = D V<sub>s</sub>²
V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> √D

answer.text: Power factor for a resistor. The power is P = V<sub>o</sub>²/R = D V<sub>s</sub>²/R. The supply current is the load current, whose RMS is V<sub>o</sub>/R = V<sub>s</sub>√D/R, so:
Comparison with phase control:

answer: Power: P = V<sub>o</sub>²/R = 115²/20 = 13 225/20 = 661.25 W. Check: at full voltage the heater takes 230²/20 = 2645 W, and 0.25 × 2645 = 661.25 W, the same.
Power factor = √0.25 = 0.5. RMS supply current = 115/20 = 5.75 A, and 230 × 5.75 × 0.5 = 661.25 W, which agrees.

Lowest frequency in the supply current: the pattern repeats every 100 cycles = 100 × 20 ms = 2 s, so the lowest component is at 1/2 = 0.5 Hz, with others at its multiples. A heater with a time constant of minutes ignores it; a lamp would blink once every two seconds.
Closing check: halving the voltage (115 V of 230 V) quarters the power, exactly as D = 0.25 says, so the answer is consistent.

bank.q: Explain TRIAC triggering with positive and negative gate pulses. Define the four triggering quadrants, state their relative sensitivity, and explain which quadrants are used by (a) positive pulses only, (b) negative pulses only, (c) a DIAC trigger. Why does the wrong choice upset a TRIAC phase controller?
outline: Terminals MT1, MT2, G; gate measured from MT1
Quadrants by MT2 and gate polarity, sketch
Q1 most sensitive, Q2 and Q3 moderate, Q4 least
Positive only: Q1 + Q4; negative only: Q2 + Q3; DIAC: Q1 + Q3
Wrong choice: late or missed firing, unequal half cycles, DC component
answer: The TRIAC. A TRIAC has main terminals MT1 and MT2 and a gate G. It behaves as two antiparallel SCRs sharing one gate, so it can be turned on whichever way MT2 is biased and conducts until its current falls below the holding current. MT1 is the reference: the polarity of MT2 and the gate current are both measured from MT1.

svg.aria: Four quadrants of TRIAC triggering by MT2 polarity and gate polarity; Q1 and Q3 shaded as the pair a DIAC uses, Q4 marked least sensitive.

answer: Sensitivity. Q1 needs the smallest gate current. Q2 and Q3 need somewhat more. Q4 (MT2 negative, gate positive) needs the most; a typical data sheet asks for about twice the Q1 value, and three-quadrant TRIACs are not rated for Q4 at all. The internal reason is that in Q4 the gate injects carriers into a region where they are less effective at starting regeneration.
In a phase controller the TRIAC must fire twice per cycle: at α with MT2 positive and at π + α with MT2 negative. The polarity of the gate pulses therefore fixes which two quadrants are used.
(a) Positive pulses only. Positive half cycle: Q1, the best quadrant. Negative half cycle: Q4, the worst. A drive sized for Q1 may fire late or not at all in Q4, so this scheme is avoided.

(b) Negative pulses only. Positive half: Q2. Negative half: Q3. Both are moderately sensitive, and the two halves behave alike. A microcontroller or logic driver does this naturally by pulling the gate below MT1, so it is the usual choice with an optocoupler or a transistor driver.

(c) DIAC trigger. The DIAC breaks over at about 30 V in either direction and passes the charge of the timing capacitor to the gate. The capacitor sits across MT2 and MT1, so its voltage, and hence the pulse, has the polarity of MT2: positive gate in the positive half (Q1), negative gate in the negative half (Q3). These are the two most sensitive quadrants.

answer.text: Summary:

answer: Why the wrong choice upsets the controller. If the TRIAC fires at α = 90° in the positive half but late, say at 120°, in the negative half, the two half cycles carry different areas. The load voltage then has a DC component and even harmonics. A lamp shows flicker; a fan motor or a transformer on the output draws a DC magnetising current that saturates its iron and overheats it. In the worst case the TRIAC misses the negative half altogether and the load sees half-wave DC.

Closing check with numbers: with a 230 V lamp of 529 Ω fired at 90° in both halves, each half delivers 25.0 W of the 50.0 W total; if the negative half is missed, only 25.0 W reaches the lamp and the current has an average value, which a symmetrical drive (b) or (c) never gives.

answer.text: The configurations:

head: Configuration
Devices
Range (R load)
Remarks
rows: three independent single-phase controllers; triplens add in the neutral
phases interact; double pulsing; usual for soft starters
cheap; unequal halves give even harmonics
each branch a single-phase controller on line voltage; SCRs carry branch current

answer: Why the three-wire star is different. With no neutral, Kirchhoff's current law at the load star point forces i<sub>a</sub> + i<sub>b</sub> + i<sub>c</sub> = 0 at every instant. A current can flow only when SCRs in at least two different lines conduct, and the star point floats: its potential is set by which lines conduct. When all three lines conduct, each resistor sees its own phase voltage; when only lines a and b conduct, each of the two resistors sees half of v<sub>ab</sub>. So the voltage on one phase depends on the switching of the other two, and the single-phase formula cannot be applied to a phase.

Firing. The SCRs are fired 60° apart in the order T1 (a +), T2 (c −), T3 (b +), T4 (a −), T5 (c +), T6 (b −), with α measured from the zero crossing of the phase voltage of T1. Because two SCRs must turn on together, each SCR gets a second pulse 60° after its first (or one wide pulse).

answer.text: Conduction modes for a resistive load:

head: α
SCRs conducting
Current
V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>ph</sub> at the end of the range

answer: Why zero at 150°. T1 can conduct with T6 through v<sub>ab</sub>, which is positive from −30° to 150°, or with T2 through v<sub>ac</sub>, positive from 30° to 210°. At α = 150° T1 and T6 are fired just as v<sub>ab</sub> reaches zero, and T1 and T2 (at α + 60° = 210°) just as v<sub>ac</sub> reaches zero, so no current can start. The four-wire star, with a return path, goes on to 180°.

Harmonics. With equal firing, the line currents of a balanced three-wire controller contain only the 6k ± 1 orders (5th, 7th, 11th, 13th). The triplens are in phase in all three lines and three-wire line currents must add to zero, so they cannot flow. In the four-wire star the triplens add in the neutral; inside a delta they circulate round the branches.

Numbers as a check: on 415 V (239.6 V per phase) with 10 Ω per phase at α = 120°, the three-wire star gives 239.6 × 0.208 = 49.8 V per phase, while three independent single-phase controllers (four-wire) would give 239.6 × 0.442 = 105.9 V. Removing the neutral more than halves the output at this angle, which is the clearest sign that the phases interact.

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 20 Ω resistor through an antiparallel SCR pair. For α = 90°, calculate the RMS output voltage, the RMS current, the power, the input power factor, and the RMS value and phase of the 50 Hz component of the supply current.
outline: V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π] with α = π/2
V<sub>o</sub> = 162.6 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 8.13 A, P = 1322.5 W
PF = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = 0.707
Fourier coefficients of the current: I<sub>1</sub> = 6.82 A lagging 32.5°
PF = displacement factor × distortion factor
answer: Data: V<sub>s</sub> = 230 V, V<sub>m</sub> = 230√2 = 325.3 V, R = 20 Ω, α = 90° = π/2 rad.
RMS output: sin 2α = sin 180° = 0, so the bracket is (π − π/2 + 0)/π = 0.5 and V<sub>o</sub> = 230 × √0.5 = 162.6 V.
RMS current: I<sub>o</sub> = 162.6/20 = 8.13 A. Power: P = I<sub>o</sub>²R = 8.13² × 20 = 1322 W (1322.5 W unrounded).
Input power factor: PF = P/(V<sub>s</sub>I<sub>o</sub>) = 1322.5/(230 × 8.13) = 0.707, which equals V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>.

answer.text: Fundamental of the current. The current is i = (V<sub>m</sub>/R) sin θ from α to π (and the negative copy in the other half). Its 50 Hz Fourier coefficients are:
answer.pre:
a<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>m</sub>/2πR)(cos 2α − 1)
b<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>m</sub>/2πR)[2(π − α) + sin 2α]
V<sub>m</sub>/R = 325.3/20 = 16.26 A
a<sub>1</sub> = (16.26/2π)(−1 − 1) = −5.18 A
b<sub>1</sub> = (16.26/2π)(π + 0) = 8.13 A
peak of fundamental = √(5.18² + 8.13²) = 9.64 A, RMS I<sub>1</sub> = 6.82 A
lag φ<sub>1</sub> = tan⁻¹(5.18/8.13) = 32.5°

answer: Displacement factor = cos 32.5° = 0.844. Distortion factor = I<sub>1</sub>/I<sub>o</sub> = 6.82/8.13 = 0.838. Their product, 0.844 × 0.838 = 0.707, is the power factor found above, which confirms both results.

Interpretation: even with a pure resistor, about half of the power-factor loss comes from the lagging fundamental (the current flows only in the second half of each half cycle) and half from the harmonics, the largest being the 150 Hz third harmonic at 3.66 A RMS, 54 % of the fundamental.

Closing check: power from the fundamental alone, V<sub>s</sub>I<sub>1</sub> cos φ<sub>1</sub> = 230 × 6.82 × 0.844 = 1324 W, matches 1322.5 W within rounding, as it must, because harmonic currents carry no power from a sinusoidal supply.

bank.q: A single-phase AC voltage controller feeds a load of R = 10 Ω and L = 31.83 mH from 230 V, 50 Hz, with wide gate pulses. For α = 90°, find the load angle, the extinction angle, the conduction angle, the RMS load voltage and current, the power and the power factor. State the control range and explain what happens at α = 30° with short pulses.
outline: Solve sin(β − φ) = sin(α − φ) exp[−(β − α)/tan φ] by trial: β = 220.9°
Range 45° to 180°; α < φ with short pulses gives one-way current
answer: Control range: φ ≤ α ≤ 180°, that is 45° to 180°. α = 90° is inside it.

answer.text: Current while T1 conducts (θ from α to β):
Extinction angle: i(β) = 0, so sin(β − 45°) = 0.7071 exp[−(β − 90°) in rad]. Trial:

answer: The sign changes between 220° and 221°. Interpolating: β = 220 + 0.0140/(0.0140 + 0.0021) = 220.9°. Conduction angle γ = β − α = 130.9° = 2.284 rad.

answer.text: RMS load voltage:
RMS load current:

answer: Power: P = I<sub>o</sub>²R = 10.12² × 10 = 1025 W. Power factor: P/(V<sub>s</sub>I<sub>o</sub>) = 1025/(230 × 10.12) = 0.440.

Compare α = 60° (the chapter example): β = 224.2°, V<sub>o</sub> = 217.1 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 14.60 A, P = 2133 W, PF = 0.635. Increasing α from 60° to 90° roughly halves the power, and β moves back only slightly, from 224.2° to 220.9°.

α = 30° with short pulses: α < φ, so when T2 is fired at 210° the current of T1 is still flowing (it would end near 225°). T1 holds T2 reverse biased, the short pulse is lost, and T2 never conducts. T1 fires every cycle, so the load current flows one way only, like a half-wave rectifier, with a DC component that would saturate a motor or transformer. A wide pulse lasting to 180° + α lets T2 fire as soon as the current of T1 ends; the current then becomes a continuous sine lagging by 45° and the load gets the full 230 V, so control is lost but nothing is damaged.
Closing check: V<sub>o</sub> = 173.6 V lies between the resistive-load value at 90° (162.6 V) and 230 V, as it should, because the inductance stretches conduction past 180°.

bank.q: A PWM AC chopper feeds a 40 Ω resistor from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply at a switching frequency of 10 kHz. Find the duty ratio for an output of 184 V RMS, the on-time, the 50 Hz part of the output, the power, and the lowest sideband. Design an input LC filter with C = 10 µF and explain how the switching frequency is chosen with respect to the filter.
outline: V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D: D = 0.64
t<sub>on</sub> = 64 µs, V<sub>1</sub> = 147.2 V, P = 846.4 W
Sidebands at m f<sub>sw</sub> ± f: lowest 9950 Hz
L = 2.53 mH for a 1 kHz corner; attenuation about 99
Trade-off between filter size and switching loss; bidirectional switches
answer: Circuit. A series bidirectional switch S1 (two IGBTs back to back) joins the supply to the load, and a freewheeling bidirectional switch S2 sits across the load. In each switching period T, S1 is on for DT and S2 for the rest.
Duty ratio: V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D, so √D = 184/230 = 0.8 and D = 0.64.
Timing: T = 1/10 000 = 100 µs and t<sub>on</sub> = 0.64 × 100 = 64 µs; the load is shorted for the other 36 µs.
50 Hz part of the output: V<sub>1</sub> = D V<sub>s</sub> = 0.64 × 230 = 147.2 V. It is smaller than the RMS value 184 V; the difference is in the switching sidebands.

Power: P = V<sub>o</sub>²/R = 184²/40 = 33 856/40 = 846.4 W. Of this, V<sub>1</sub>²/R = 147.2²/40 = 541.7 W is at 50 Hz and 304.7 W in the sidebands, which a resistor heater uses but a motor would not.

Sidebands: the output is v<sub>s</sub> times a switching function of frequency f<sub>sw</sub>, so the unwanted frequencies are m·f<sub>sw</sub> ± 50 Hz: 9950 Hz and 10 050 Hz, then 19 950 Hz and 20 050 Hz, and so on. The lowest is 9950 Hz.

answer.text: Input filter. Without it, the supply current is the pulsed load current, power factor √D = 0.8. An LC low-pass between supply and chopper with corner frequency f<sub>c</sub> well between 50 Hz and 9950 Hz removes the pulses. Choose f<sub>c</sub> = 1 kHz with C = 10 µF:

answer: Supply current with the filter: the supply delivers the 50 Hz average D × 230/40 = 0.64 × 5.75 = 3.68 A in phase (check: 230 × 3.68 = 846.4 W), plus the capacitor current 230/318.3 = 0.72 A leading. Total √(3.68² + 0.72²) = 3.75 A, power factor 3.68/3.75 = 0.98.

Choosing f<sub>sw</sub>. The filter must pass 50 Hz and stop f<sub>sw</sub> − 50 Hz, so the higher f<sub>sw</sub>, the higher the corner can be and the smaller L and C become (each about in proportion to 1/f<sub>sw</sub>). But each switching event costs energy, so switching loss rises about in proportion to f<sub>sw</sub>, and so does interference. Below about 20 kHz the inductor may whine. IGBT choppers usually settle between 5 kHz and 20 kHz; SiC devices allow higher.
Closing check: √0.64 × 230 = 0.8 × 230 = 184 V, the required output.

bank.q: A single-phase step-down cycloconverter using two bridge converter groups is to produce a 12.5 Hz output of 120 V RMS (fundamental) from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply into an inductive load, using cosine-wave crossing. Explain the firing-angle pattern of each group, find the modulation ratio and the firing angles at output angles 0°, 30°, 60° and 90°, and sketch the output.
outline: f<sub>o</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> = 1/4: one output cycle = four supply cycles; each output half = four supply half cycles
P group for the positive half, N group for the negative half
α = cos⁻¹(r sin ω<sub>o</sub>t), largest fundamental peak 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 207.1 V
Changeover at current zero or with circulating current
answer: Frequencies: f<sub>o</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> = 12.5/50 = 1/4. One output period is 80 ms, four supply periods; each output half cycle (40 ms) contains four supply half cycles. 12.5 Hz is below the usual limit f<sub>s</sub>/3 = 16.7 Hz, so the waveform quality is acceptable.

Groups. The P group (a single-phase bridge) carries the positive load current and makes the positive output half cycle; the N group (a second bridge in antiparallel) makes the negative half. In non-circulating mode the N group is released only after the load current has fallen to zero and a short dead time has passed.

answer.text: Cosine-wave crossing. A reference V<sub>r</sub> sin ω<sub>o</sub>t is compared with a cosine timing wave V<sub>c</sub> cos ωt locked to the supply; firing at the crossing gives cos α = r sin ω<sub>o</sub>t. With continuous current, each supply half cycle then contributes an average
answer.pre: v<sub>avg</sub> = (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α = (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) r sin ω<sub>o</sub>t

answer: Largest output: V<sub>m</sub> = 230√2 = 325.3 V, so 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 207.1 V peak, or 146.4 V RMS, at r = 1.
Modulation ratio: the wanted peak is 120√2 = 169.7 V, so r = 169.7/207.1 = 0.820.

answer.text: Firing angles of the P group:

answer: Pattern. Through the positive output half cycle α falls from 90° towards 35.0° at the output peak and rises back to 90° at the end; past the zero the N group repeats the same pattern, so its pieces average to the negative half sine. Within one supply half cycle α changes little, so each piece is a phase-controlled section of the rectified supply.

Sketch: draw the 50 Hz supply dashed over 80 ms. On it draw the output as pieces of the rectified supply (each starting at its α) for 0 to 40 ms, positive, and as pieces of the inverted rectified supply for 40 to 80 ms, negative. Through the pieces draw the 12.5 Hz sine of peak 169.7 V that their averages follow. The load current, smoothed by the inductance, is close to a 12.5 Hz sine lagging the voltage.
Input power factor: the input current lags by roughly α, so near the output zeros (α near 90°) the displacement factor is poor; the average over the cycle is low unless r is near 1.
Closing check: at the output peak, 207.1 × cos 35.0° = 207.1 × 0.820 = 169.8 V, the wanted peak within rounding.

bank.q: A three-phase to three-phase matrix converter uses nine bidirectional switches. Explain the switching constraints and the number of allowed states, state and justify the maximum voltage transfer ratio, find the highest output line voltage available from a 400 V supply, and find the duty cycles of output A that give an average of 150 V at an instant when input a is at its positive peak.
outline: S<sub>Xy</sub> joins input y to output X; two IGBTs per switch, 18 in all
Never two switches on one output; never none
27 states: 6 + 18 + 3
q ≤ √3/2 from the narrowest input gap 1.5 V<sub>im</sub>
346 V line; d<sub>Aa</sub> = 0.640, d<sub>Ab</sub> = d<sub>Ac</sub> = 0.180
answer: Structure. Inputs a, b, c come through an LC filter; outputs A, B, C go to the load. Switch S<sub>Xy</sub> joins input y to output X. Each is bidirectional: two IGBTs joined emitter to emitter with antiparallel diodes, so there are 18 IGBTs.
Constraint 1: never close two switches feeding the same output. S<sub>Aa</sub> and S<sub>Ab</sub> together connect input a to input b through output A: a line-to-line short circuit.
Constraint 2: never open all three switches of an output. The load is inductive, so its current must always have a path; interrupting it gives a destructive voltage spike.

States. Exactly one switch per output is closed, so each output has 3 choices and there are 3³ = 27 states: 6 in which the outputs take three different inputs, 18 in which two outputs share one input, and 3 zero states with all outputs on the same input.

answer.text: Maximum transfer ratio. Over a switching period an output voltage is a weighted mix of the three input voltages, so every output line voltage must fit inside the gap between the highest and lowest input voltage at that instant. With input phase peak V<sub>im</sub>:
answer.pre:
gap = max(v<sub>a</sub>, v<sub>b</sub>, v<sub>c</sub>) − min(v<sub>a</sub>, v<sub>b</sub>, v<sub>c</sub>)
largest gap  = √3 V<sub>im</sub>  (two inputs at ±0.866 V<sub>im</sub>)
smallest gap = 1.5 V<sub>im</sub>  (one input at V<sub>im</sub>, two at −0.5 V<sub>im</sub>)
output line peak √3 V<sub>om</sub> ≤ 1.5 V<sub>im</sub>  so  V<sub>om</sub> ≤ 0.866 V<sub>im</sub>

answer: So q = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>in</sub> ≤ √3/2 = 0.866. The basic Venturini method reaches only 0.5; injecting third harmonics into the input and output references reaches 0.866.
Highest output from 400 V: output line voltage = 0.866 × 400 = 346 V RMS, or 200 V RMS per phase.

answer.text: Duty cycles at the instant: input phase peak = 400√2/√3 = 326.6 V, so v<sub>a</sub> = 326.6 V and v<sub>b</sub> = v<sub>c</sub> = −163.3 V. Taking d<sub>Ab</sub> = d<sub>Ac</sub>:

answer: With a 10 kHz switching frequency (T<sub>s</sub> = 100 µs) these are on-times of 64.0 µs, 18.0 µs and 18.0 µs, adding to 100 µs so output A is never left open.
Closing check: 0.640 × 326.6 + 0.360 × (−163.3) = 209.0 − 58.8 = 150.2 V, the wanted 150 V within rounding.

bank.q: A 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply feeds a star-connected resistive load of 40 Ω per phase through three antiparallel SCR pairs, with the neutral connected. For α = 120°, find the RMS phase voltage, the phase current, and the total power. Repeat with the neutral removed and explain the difference.
outline: With neutral: single-phase formula per phase
Without neutral: 90° to 150° formula; V<sub>o</sub> = 48.0 V; 1.20 A; 173 W
Reason: no return path, two lines must conduct, zero at 150°
answer: Supply phase voltage: V<sub>ph</sub> = 400/√3 = 230.9 V. α = 120° = 2π/3 rad.

answer.text: With the neutral, each phase is an independent single-phase controller:

answer: Phase current = 102.1/40 = 2.55 A. Power per phase = 102.1²/40 = 260.7 W; total = 3 × 260.7 = 782 W. The neutral carries the triplen harmonics of the three phase currents.

answer.text: Without the neutral, the load is a three-wire star and α = 120° lies in the 90° to 150° range:

answer: Phase current = 48.0/40 = 1.20 A. Total power = 3 × 48.0²/40 = 173 W.

Why the difference. With the neutral, each SCR pair conducts from 120° to 180° of its own phase voltage. Without it, current flows only when SCRs in two lines conduct together, and the line-to-line voltage between those lines is near its end: the pair T1, T6 is fired at 120° but v<sub>ab</sub> falls to zero at 150°, so each pulse of current is short. The output falls to zero at α = 150° instead of 180°.
The balanced three-wire load still has equal phase voltages; what changes is their size and shape, and the line currents now carry no triplen harmonics.
Closing check: the ratio of the two powers, 173/782 = 0.22, equals (0.208/0.442)², as it must for the same resistors.

bank.q: Compare phase control, integral-cycle control and PWM AC chopping for a 1 kW lamp dimmer on a 230 V supply, on harmonics, power factor, flicker, noise and filter needs, with numbers at half power. Recommend one for a domestic dimmer and justify.
outline: Half power: α = 90°, D = 0.5, chopper D = 0.5
Phase control: PF 0.707, 3rd harmonic 54 %, smooth, cheap, RFI
On-off: PF 0.707, subharmonics, visible flicker
PWM: PF near 1 with filter, sidebands at kHz, more devices
Recommendation: TRIAC phase control with an EMI choke and snubber
answer: Load: a 1 kW lamp at 230 V has R = 230²/1000 = 52.9 Ω (taken constant). Half power, 500 W, needs V<sub>o</sub> = 230 × √0.5 = 162.6 V RMS in every scheme.

Phase control at half power needs α = 90° (bracket 0.5). The current is a chopped sine of RMS 162.6/52.9 = 3.07 A. Its fundamental lags by 32.5° and its third harmonic is 54 % of the fundamental, so PF = 0.707. Switching at the peak of the voltage causes a fast current step, which radiates radio interference and can make the lamp filament buzz; an EMI choke and a snubber are needed. Control is smooth, every half cycle.

Integral-cycle control at half power needs D = 0.5, for example 5 cycles on and 5 off. PF = √0.5 = 0.707 as well, there are no 150 Hz harmonics and hardly any interference, because switching is at the voltage zero. But the pattern repeats every 0.2 s, so the lamp blinks at 5 Hz, which the eye sees very clearly. Using 1 on and 1 off raises the blink to 25 Hz, still visible as flicker on a filament lamp.

PWM chopper at half power: the RMS output is V<sub>s</sub>√D, so D = 0.5 gives 162.6 V into the lamp. The unwanted frequencies sit at f<sub>sw</sub> ± 50 Hz, for example 9950 Hz at 10 kHz, so a small LC input filter makes the supply current nearly sinusoidal and in phase: PF close to 1 instead of 0.707. It needs four IGBTs with gate drives, a controller and the filter, and it has switching losses and some audible noise below 20 kHz.

answer.text: Comparison at half power:

head: Feature
Phase control
Integral cycle
PWM chopper
rows: SCRs or TRIAC with a zero-cross driver
four IGBTs, driver, controller, LC filter

answer: Integral-cycle control is ruled out for lighting by flicker. Between the other two, the domestic dimmer is a small load (1 kW): its low power factor and third harmonic cost the user nothing on a household tariff and are within what the supply tolerates for one appliance, while price and size matter a great deal.

Recommendation: a TRIAC phase controller with an RC-DIAC trigger (or a microcontroller with negative-pulse drive), plus an EMI choke and an RC snubber. It gives smooth, flicker-free dimming with about five parts. A PWM chopper is worth its cost only where harmonic limits or power factor are enforced, for example many dimmers in a theatre or a commercial building, where their 150 Hz currents add up in the neutral.
Closing check: all three schemes deliver the same 500 W at 162.6 V RMS; they differ only in how the supply sees the current and how the eye sees the light.

bank.q: Distinguish the circulating-current and non-circulating-current modes of a cycloconverter. Discuss the effect of each on output waveform quality, the intergroup reactor, changeover time, efficiency and control.
outline: Circulating: both groups fired, α<sub>P</sub> + α<sub>N</sub> = 180°, intergroup reactor
Smooth changeover, continuous current, extra loss and size
Non-circulating: one group at a time, dead time at current zero
No reactor, better efficiency, distortion near changeover
Choice by output frequency and rating
answer: Background. A cycloconverter has a P group for positive load current and an N group for negative current, connected in antiparallel. The question is what the idle group does while the other conducts.

Circulating-current mode. Both groups are fired all the time, with α<sub>P</sub> + α<sub>N</sub> = 180°, so their average output voltages are equal: (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α<sub>P</sub> = −(2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α<sub>N</sub>. Their instantaneous voltages are not equal, so a current circulates through the two groups. An intergroup reactor (often centre-tapped) between them absorbs the instantaneous voltage difference and limits this current.

Effects of the circulating mode: the load current can reverse at any instant, because both groups are ready, so the changeover is instantaneous and the output follows the reference smoothly with no dead time. Both groups conduct continuously, so even light loads see continuous current and a predictable output voltage. Against this, the reactor is large and heavy, it and the thyristors carry the circulating current in addition to the load current, so losses rise and efficiency falls, and the input power factor gets worse.

Non-circulating mode. Only the group that must carry the present load current is fired; the other gets no pulses. When the reference calls for a change of current direction, the controller removes the pulses of the outgoing group, waits until the load current has fallen to zero, adds a short dead time (a millisecond or so) so the outgoing thyristors regain their blocking ability, and then fires the incoming group.

Effects of the non-circulating mode: no reactor is needed and no circulating current flows, so the equipment is smaller and more efficient. But during each dead time the load current is held at zero, which flattens the current waveform around its zero crossings and distorts the output; at light load the current becomes discontinuous and the output voltage no longer follows the cosine law. The control needs a reliable zero-current detector: firing the incoming group too early shorts the supply through the two groups.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
Circulating current
Non-circulating
rows: after current zero plus dead time
short circuit if the zero is misjudged

answer: Choice. Circulating mode suits drives that reverse current often or need very smooth low-frequency torque, where the waveform matters more than the losses. Non-circulating mode is the common choice for large mill and kiln drives, where efficiency and size dominate and the dead time is small compared with the long output period: at 5 Hz the output period is 200 ms, so a 1 ms dead time hardly shows.
Closing check: in both modes the average output of the working group is (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α, so on a 230 V supply neither can give more than 207.1 V peak of fundamental.

bank.q: A 5 Hz to 20 Hz, 400 V three-phase induction motor drive is to be fed from a 50 Hz, 400 V supply. Evaluate three options: a cycloconverter, a matrix converter, and a rectifier with a DC link and PWM inverter. Choose one for (a) a 5 MW ore mill and (b) a 20 kW conveyor that brakes often, and justify with device count, voltage, power factor, frequency range and regeneration.
outline: Cycloconverter: 36 SCRs, f<sub>o</sub> ≤ 16.7 Hz, poor input PF at low voltage, very high power
Matrix: 18 IGBTs, q ≤ 0.866 (346 V from 400 V), sinusoidal input, natural regeneration
DC link: 6 diodes + 6 IGBTs, any frequency, full voltage, capacitor, no regeneration without active front end
Mill: cycloconverter; conveyor: matrix or active front end
Scoring table
answer: Requirement. Output 5 Hz to 20 Hz at up to 400 V line, from a 400 V, 50 Hz supply. At 20 Hz the motor needs only about 20/50 × 400 = 160 V for constant flux, so the voltage need is modest at the low end.

Cycloconverter. A three-phase to three-phase cycloconverter with six-pulse bridge groups uses 36 thyristors (18 with three-pulse groups). Thyristors are cheap, rugged and available in very large ratings, and commutation is natural, so it suits multi-megawatt drives. Its limits: good waveforms only up to about f<sub>s</sub>/3 = 16.7 Hz, so the top of the 5 Hz to 20 Hz range is outside the comfortable zone; the input power factor is poor whenever the output voltage is low (α near 90°), as it is at 5 Hz; and the input current carries harmonics and interharmonics. It regenerates, because each group can invert.

Matrix converter. Nine bidirectional switches, 18 IGBTs. Any output frequency, including 20 Hz, with a small LC input filter giving a near-sinusoidal input current at unity power factor, and natural regeneration. Its limit is q ≤ 0.866: from 400 V the most it gives is 0.866 × 400 = 346 V line, enough for 20 Hz (160 V) but not for a 400 V motor at 50 Hz. It has no DC-link capacitor, so it is compact, but it cannot ride through supply dips and needs four-step commutation.

Rectifier, DC link and PWM inverter. Six diodes, a DC-link capacitor and six IGBTs. Any frequency from 0 to well above 50 Hz, full output voltage, mature control and the lowest cost at small and medium power. A diode rectifier cannot return braking energy, so a braking resistor (energy wasted) or an active front end (six more IGBTs, total 12) is needed. The capacitor is bulky and ages, and the diode rectifier draws a distorted input current.

answer.text: Scoring (3 = best):

head: Criterion
Cycloconverter
Matrix
DC link + PWM inverter
rows: 6 diodes + 6 IGBTs (12 IGBTs with active front end)
2 with diode front end, 3 with active front end

answer: (a) 5 MW ore mill at 5 Hz to 20 Hz. The speed is low, the torque enormous and the power in megawatts, where thyristors are the cheapest and most robust switches. Most of the time the mill runs at its low design speed, well inside f<sub>s</sub>/3. A cycloconverter (in practice feeding a gearless synchronous motor) is the established choice; a reactive-power compensator usually corrects its poor input power factor. Choose the cycloconverter, accepting reduced quality near 20 Hz.

(b) 20 kW conveyor that brakes often. The power is small, the full 5 Hz to 20 Hz range is needed, and braking energy should be returned rather than burnt. Both the matrix converter and a DC-link drive with an active front end meet this. The matrix converter is more compact and needs no electrolytic capacitor, and its 346 V limit is no handicap because the motor needs only 160 V at 20 Hz. The active-front-end drive is cheaper and more familiar to maintain. Choose the matrix converter if size and capacitor life matter, otherwise the active-front-end drive; the cycloconverter is not suitable at 20 kW.

Closing check: the voltage needed at the top speed (160 V at 20 Hz) is below the matrix limit of 346 V, and 20 Hz is above the cycloconverter guideline of 16.7 Hz, which is why the two recommendations differ.

bank.q: Derive the input power factor of a single-phase phase-controlled AC voltage controller with a resistive load as a function of α, and split it into displacement and distortion factors at α = 90°. Discuss how its harmonic currents affect the supply transformer and the neutral of a three-phase four-wire installation, with numbers for three 20 Ω loads on 230 V at α = 90°.
outline: PF = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = √[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π]
Fundamental lags: at 90°, DF = 0.844, distortion factor = 0.838
Odd harmonics, 3rd 54 % of fundamental at 90°
Neutral: triplens add, 11.5 A against 8.13 A phase current
Transformer: extra losses, derating; remedies

answer.text: Power factor. For a resistor the supply current is the load current, of RMS V<sub>o</sub>/R, and P = V<sub>o</sub>²/R:
answer.pre:
PF = P/(V<sub>s</sub>I<sub>s</sub>) = (V<sub>o</sub>²/R)/(V<sub>s</sub> × V<sub>o</sub>/R) = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>
PF(α) = √[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π]

answer.text: Displacement factor. The current flows from α to π in each half cycle, later than the voltage, so its 50 Hz part lags. With V<sub>m</sub>/R as the scale:
answer.pre:
a<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>m</sub>/2πR)(cos 2α − 1),  b<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>m</sub>/2πR)[2(π − α) + sin 2α]
at α = 90°: a<sub>1</sub> = −(V<sub>m</sub>/R)/π, b<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>m</sub>/R)/2
lag φ<sub>1</sub> = tan⁻¹(0.318/0.5) = 32.5°,  displacement factor = cos 32.5° = 0.844

answer: Distortion factor. The fundamental peak is (V<sub>m</sub>/R)√(0.318² + 0.5²) = 0.593 V<sub>m</sub>/R, RMS 0.419 V<sub>m</sub>/R; the total RMS current is 0.5 V<sub>m</sub>/R. Distortion factor = 0.419/0.5 = 0.838. Check: 0.844 × 0.838 = 0.707 = PF at 90°. So a phase controller lowers the power factor through both a lagging fundamental and harmonics; it is wrong to say its displacement factor is unity.

answer.text: Harmonics of one 20 Ω load on 230 V at α = 90° (V<sub>m</sub>/R = 16.26 A); the waveform has half-wave symmetry, so only odd orders appear:

answer: Neutral of a four-wire system. Put one such load on each phase of a 400/230 V four-wire supply. The fundamentals and the 5th and 7th harmonics are 120° apart in the three phases and cancel in the neutral, but the triplens (3rd, 9th, …) are in phase in all three and add. The 3rd alone gives 3 × 3.66 = 11.0 A; adding all triplens, the neutral carries 11.5 A RMS, more than the 8.13 A in each phase. A neutral sized like, or smaller than, the phase conductors can overheat although every phase is within its rating.

Supply transformer. Harmonic currents raise the winding eddy-current and stray losses, which grow roughly with the square of frequency, so the transformer runs hotter than its kVA reading suggests and must be derated. In a delta-star distribution transformer the triplens circulate in the delta winding and add heating there. Harmonic currents through the source impedance also distort the voltage seen by other consumers.

Remedies: a neutral conductor sized for the triplen current; a delta winding or zigzag transformer to trap triplens; passive filters tuned near the 3rd and 5th harmonics; on-off control for heaters, which has no 150 Hz component; or a PWM AC chopper with an input filter, whose supply current is nearly sinusoidal.
Closing check: the squares of the harmonic table add to the total, 6.82² + 3.66² + 1.22² + 1.22² + 0.73² + … ≈ 8.13², so the Fourier values are consistent with the 8.13 A RMS current.

glossary.def: A thyristor switch in series with an AC load that varies the RMS load voltage at the supply frequency; also called an AC voltage regulator.
Delaying the turn-on of the thyristors by the firing angle α in every half cycle, so only part of each half sine reaches the load.
The angle from the zero crossing of the supply voltage to the gate pulse.
The angle at which the load current returns to zero and the SCR turns off; π for a resistor, more than π for an RL load.
The angle for which an SCR conducts, β − α; π − α for a resistive load.
tan⁻¹(ωL/R) for a series R-L load; the smallest useful firing angle.
Passing n whole supply cycles and blocking m whole cycles, switching at the voltage zero.
In on-off control, n/(n + m); in a PWM AC chopper, t<sub>on</sub>/T.
A frequency component below the supply frequency, such as the 50/(n + m) Hz of on-off control.
A bidirectional three-terminal thyristor (MT1, MT2, gate) that behaves like two antiparallel SCRs with one gate.
A two-terminal bidirectional trigger device that breaks over at about 30 V and dumps a capacitor charge into a gate.
One of the four combinations of MT2 polarity and gate-current polarity of a TRIAC, both measured from MT1.
The main current that must flow as the gate pulse ends for a thyristor to stay on.
The current below which a conducting thyristor turns off; smaller than the latching current.
The rate of rise of voltage across a TRIAC just after its current reaches zero; too fast a rise turns it back on.
A series RC network across a switch that limits dv/dt and prevents false triggering.
An LED and a light-fired TRIAC in one package, used to drive a power TRIAC from isolated logic; random-phase or zero-crossing types.
Giving each SCR of a three-phase controller a second gate pulse 60° after the first, so two SCRs in different lines conduct together.
Harmonics of order 3, 9, 15, …; in a balanced three-phase system they are in phase in all three lines (zero sequence).
A three-phase AC voltage controller that raises the voltage of an induction motor gradually to limit the starting current.
An AC voltage controller that switches the load between the supply and a short at several kilohertz, with series and freewheeling bidirectional switches.
A switch that blocks voltage and carries current in both directions, usually two IGBTs joined emitter to emitter with antiparallel diodes.
A direct AC-AC frequency changer made of two phase-controlled converter groups in antiparallel, with no DC link.
Firing control in which an SCR fires where a reference sine meets a cosine timing wave, so that cos α follows the reference.
An inductor between the two groups of a circulating-current cycloconverter that limits the circulating current.
A direct AC-AC converter with nine bidirectional switches that join any input line to any output line.
Output to input phase voltage ratio of a matrix converter; at most √3/2 = 0.866 in the linear range.
The four-stage gate sequence, based on the sign of the load current, that moves a matrix-converter output from one input to another without a short or an open load.
